title: What Happens When You Open a Website?

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities
sources.notes: Checked resolver, hierarchy and cache behavior; narrative uses a deliberately simplified uncached lookup.

sources.title: RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1
sources.notes: Checked request/response framing and connection management; this episode uses a teaching example of HTTP/1.1 over TCP.

sources.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
sources.notes: Checked ports, sequence numbers and connection establishment.

sources.title: RFC 9114: HTTP/3
sources.notes: Checked HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC rather than TCP.

sections.title: One click, many conversations
sections.narration: You click a website, and the loading circle starts its little workout. What is everyone waiting for? Let's follow one request and see the team effort hiding behind that single click.
sections.takeaway: Opening a website is a sequence of coordinated network tasks.

sections.title: Choose a clear teaching model
sections.narration: We'll use a simple example: HTTP version one point one over TCP. Real browsers have shortcuts, like saved answers and reused connections. For now, we're taking the scenic route so we can see each step.
sections.takeaway: This example explains one path, not every modern browser connection.

sections.title: From LAN to WAN
sections.narration: First, our request leaves the local network. Routers help it reach other networks. Think of campus buildings connected by roads: the Internet joins lots of separate networks, rather than being one giant room.
sections.takeaway: The Internet connects many separate networks.

sections.title: Layers divide the work
sections.narration: These layers are a way to split the jobs. OSI lists seven; this TCP/IP model groups them into four. Same general responsibilities, different grouping. It's a team chart, not seven physical boxes inside your laptop.
sections.takeaway: OSI and TCP/IP group related communication responsibilities differently.

sections.title: Ask for an address
sections.narration: We know the website's name, but where does it live? DNS helps us find its address. Our browser asks a helper called a resolver. Basically: 'I know the name. Can you find the place?'
sections.takeaway: DNS helps translate a useful name into addressing information.

sections.title: Follow the DNS hierarchy
sections.narration: If the resolver has no saved answer, it follows directions: root, top-level domain, then the server responsible for that name. Like asking around campus, each reply gets us closer. The resolver does the running around.
sections.takeaway: An uncached DNS lookup may follow several referrals.

sections.title: Reuse a cached answer
sections.narration: Good news: we don't always repeat that whole search. The resolver can save an answer in its cache. But saved answers have an expiry time. Even a helpful shortcut needs a freshness check.
sections.takeaway: A cached DNS answer can shorten the next visit.

sections.title: Choose the receiving process
sections.narration: An IP address gets us to the host. A port helps find the right application there. Here, client port 49152 talks to server port 80. Think building address first, then the right room.
sections.takeaway: An IP address alone does not select the receiving application.

sections.title: Establish a TCP connection
sections.narration: Before sending our request, TCP does a quick three-message introduction: SYN, SYN with ACK, then ACK. Both sides set up their connection state. They haven't booked a private cable across the Internet, though.
sections.takeaway: The TCP handshake establishes connection state at both ends.

sections.title: Build the HTTP request
sections.narration: Now comes GET: 'Please send me this resource.' HTTP gives that request its meaning. TCP carries the bytes underneath. It's like a delivery service that moves your assignment without checking whether your answers are correct.
sections.takeaway: HTTP describes what the application wants.

sections.title: Wrap the application bytes
sections.narration: Keep your eye on the blue message. We're adding information around it, like putting a letter inside labelled envelopes. That's encapsulation. And a big message may need several transport segments to make the trip.
sections.takeaway: Encapsulation packages one layer's data for the next layer.

sections.title: Transport adds its information
sections.narration: The TCP information includes ports and sequence numbers. That helps identify the endpoints and track the bytes. Our HTTP message stays inside. One application's write doesn't have to fit neatly inside one TCP segment.
sections.takeaway: TCP organizes a byte stream into segments for transmission.

sections.title: Address the IP packet
sections.narration: Now we add the IP information: where the data is coming from and where it's going. Routers use it to pick the next hop. Our server stays the goal, although address translation can change addresses.
sections.takeaway: IP addressing supports delivery across interconnected networks.

sections.title: Prepare the local frame
sections.narration: The outermost envelope handles the next local step. For a distant server, that step might be our gateway. The server's IP is the final destination; the local MAC address helps us reach the next stop.
sections.takeaway: A link-layer frame serves one local link.

sections.title: Turn bits into signals
sections.narration: Tiny written zeros and ones aren't actually running through the cable. Those bits become changing signals. A wire, a fiber, and a radio link carry them differently. The picture is showing the idea, not miniature travelling digits.
sections.takeaway: Physical transmission carries encoded information over a medium.

sections.title: The switch forwards a frame
sections.narration: Here's the switch. It uses MAC forwarding information to choose a local outgoing port. Its job is more like directing traffic inside one area. Choosing a route between different networks is a different job.
sections.takeaway: A switch forwards within its link-layer domain.

sections.title: The router chooses a next hop
sections.narration: The router opens the local envelope, checks the IP destination, and picks the next hop. It doesn't need to read our HTTP request. You don't need to read a parcel's contents to follow its address.
sections.takeaway: Routers connect networks by forwarding IP packets.

sections.title: New frame, continuing packet
sections.narration: Notice that the local envelope changes at each routed hop. The request is still heading toward our server. Like changing buses on a journey, each local step has its own connection details.
sections.takeaway: Link-layer envelopes are replaced as a packet crosses routers.

sections.title: Shared links can queue or lose
sections.narration: Our packet has company. Other traffic needs that outgoing link too, so packets can form a queue. When the queue fills, new arrivals may get dropped. The Internet also has its version of a canteen rush.
sections.takeaway: Packets share limited resources along the path.

sections.title: Unwrap at the server
sections.narration: We've reached the server. Now the unpacking goes upward: handle the local frame, then IP, then TCP, and finally pass the HTTP bytes to the application. Every layer deals with its own part of the delivery.
sections.takeaway: Decapsulation lets each receiving layer perform its own job.

sections.title: Send an HTTP response
sections.narration: The server sends a response back, including status information and content. The return journey uses the layers too. It doesn't have to follow exactly the same route. Getting home can involve a different set of roads.
bullets: The response takes a return path
sections.takeaway: The server sends a new application message back.

sections.title: A page can trigger more requests
sections.narration: Plot twist: that first response may only be the start. The HTML can ask for styles and images, so more requests follow. Some resources may come from caches or other servers. One page, quite a group project.
sections.takeaway: One visible page can require many resource transfers.
sections.short_title: Fetch the rest of the page

sections.title: Add the modern distinctions
sections.narration: One final update: HTTPS adds TLS protection, and HTTP version three uses QUIC over UDP. So our TCP journey is one example, not every browser connection. The basic jobs of addressing and moving data still remain.
sections.takeaway: The web uses several protocol combinations, not only HTTP over TCP.

sections.title: Retell the whole journey
sections.narration: So that one click needed a name lookup, connection setup, a request, several network steps, and some unpacking. Try spotting the difference between a website name, an IP address, a port, and the next local address.
sections.takeaway: A page load succeeds because multiple protocols perform distinct jobs.
